title: Review, Refinement History and Retrospective
body: ## Review, Refinement History and Retrospective `REVIEW.md` is the **honest record of what happened**. It links the promised `AC-##` criteria to actual automated evidence, human playtest observations and the final Gate A verdict. ### When to use Use during technical verification, after a human tries a build, when defects lead to another round and at sprint closure or handoff. ### One result per criterion For each actual `AC-##` in `SPRINT.md`, record: - `result: pass | fail | partial | not_tested`; - method: automated, manual-playtest or manual-inspection; - who performed it (agent, human, CI, or unknown); - actual environment/device where known; - real source of evidence and concise notes. Don't fill `performed_by: human` unless the human actually reports their observation. A screenshot generated by automation isn't a substitute for their experience. ### A useful playtest instruction “Launch the verified build, use arrows to move the duck toward each arena edge, then let a hazard collide. Does movement stop at the border? Can you identify hazards before impact? Does restart give control back?” This is specific, short and tied to the original criteria. Avoid asking the user to complete a huge survey merely to exercise Gate A. ### Refinement rounds Use `round-1`, `round-2` and so on to preserve: 1. trigger and observed failure; 2. diagnosis and uncertainty; 3. corrected or revised plan, and whether a new Gate I was needed; 4. actual source/test changes; 5. subsequent human retest and verdict. **Do not overwrite old negative feedback.** A later successful round means the sprint improved; it does not mean earlier testing never failed. ### Accepted with conditions Conditional acceptance must list specific conditions, affected criteria and any unresolved release blockers. The sprint is not unconditionally releasable while blocking conditions remain. Follow the normalized status/approval rules in the Sprint File Contract rather than assuming all “accepted” labels mean the same thing. ### Retrospective A short retrospective captures: - intended versus observed outcome; - design hypothesis that the experiment supported or disproved; - technical or player-experience lessons; - deferred work and newly discovered risks; - next **proposed** sprint, not an automatically authorized one. The learning outcome should be **observed or marked unverified**, not a claim that the user understood a concept simply because the agent explained it. ### Example: a hard-to-see hazard In `round-1`, the human reports low contrast and Gate A says `needs_refinement`. The agent corrects a visual cue inside approved scope, reruns tests and records `round-2`. The human retests. Only the **actual** new verdict can close the sprint. ### Common failures **Review after the fact:** No acceptance criteria were defined before source changes. Improve planning next sprint. **Paper acceptance:** Tests pass and the agent fills human verdict. Keep pending. **Lost handoff:** The next agent cannot tell which round is active. Update `STATE.md` and the review record. ### Related [Playtesting](#wiki-quality--playtesting) · [Acceptance stage](#wiki-lifecycle--acceptance) · [Resumption](#wiki-agents--handoff)

title: Guided Discovery: Ask Less, Decide Better
body: ## Guided Discovery: Ask Less, Decide Better The point of guided discovery is not to make an AI more chatty. It's to help a designer transform uncertainty into **small, informed, human-owned choices** while maintaining a usable project record. ### When to use Use for new game ideas, an uncertain mechanic, a student who is learning design, or a returning developer unsure how to approach the next playable feature. ### One meaningful question at a time The default pace is a **single consequential question** per turn. A batch of up to three related questions can be useful if the person opts for faster intake, but avoid demanding ten independent preferences before showing anything useful. Ask a question *because an immediate decision depends on it*. “Would you prefer direct or inertia-based movement?” is actionable. “What is your favorite color and music genre?” is probably not actionable while movement hasn't been tested. ### The discovery ladder 1. **Player verb:** move, aim, rotate, trade, negotiate, connect, select, build, hide? 2. **System response:** how does the world visibly react to that verb? 3. **Player feedback:** can a novice tell what changed and why? 4. **Smallest experiment:** which five-minute playable slice will test the hypothesis? 5. **Important fork:** which difference might materially change the player's experience? 6. **Human choice:** select, defer, reject or request more evidence. 7. **Durable record:** agent updates `GAME.md`, `DECISIONS.md`, backlog and the active sprint. Don't march through all seven as a form. Use only what the user's current answer and goal require. ### Option design When proposing concepts, ensure choices differ **mechanically**. Avoid three identical dodge games wearing different themes. For each option, include one action, one response, one smallest prototype and one uncertain tradeoff. Recommend an option when helpful, but label it clearly as a recommendation. “I don't know” should lead to a **reversible experiment or focused research**, not forced agreement. ### Example — level design learning A student wants to teach a player a new jump ability. The agent offers: - a low-risk introductory gap with safe recovery; - a timed obstacle requiring the jump immediately. It explains onboarding, failure cost and feedback tradeoffs, and asks which one the student wants to prototype first. Later the playtest should reveal whether a player notices the jump cue. That's an observable learning checkpoint. ### Recording without bureaucracy A selected significant choice becomes a `D-###` entry with context, options and actual human response. A minor parameter inside an already approved technical plan may remain a routine T0 detail. The agent shouldn't force the user to hand-write either record. ### Common failures **AI decides everything:** The agent presents a complete game design and asks for one approval. Break it into material choices. **Indecision loop:** The assistant asks unlimited open questions. Offer a bounded experiment. **Learning by lecture:** The agent explains theory without tying it to a gameplay test. Create a prediction and observation instead. ### Related [Learning checkpoints](#wiki-learning--checkpoints) · [Decision records](#wiki-learning--decisions) · [No-idea start](#wiki-guides--from-zero)

title: Learning Checkpoints Through Playable Evidence
body: ## Learning Checkpoints Through Playable Evidence ADDF Light Games includes learning because the human should understand the *design and engineering consequences* of the decisions the AI helps implement. ### When to use Use when teaching game mechanics, systems or level design, onboarding a nonprogrammer, or deciding which experiment to build next. A checkpoint is especially valuable when two alternatives have different player-facing tradeoffs. ### The six-part pattern 1. **Concept:** One relevant principle in accessible language. 2. **Concrete example:** How this principle appears in this game. 3. **Tradeoff:** Two legitimate approaches, not a false choice. 4. **Prediction:** What the designer expects to notice during play. 5. **Test:** A real playable or observable experiment with relevant acceptance criteria. 6. **Reflection:** Actual observations, uncertainty and any new decision. No quiz score or compulsory “correct answer” is necessary. If the user wants only the implementation summary, keep the explanation short and provide a deeper link. ### Mechanic design example **Concept:** Control feel depends on acceleration and stopping behavior. **Options:** Direct speed gives predictable response; easing/acceleration can feel weightier but needs tuning and can mask collision mistakes. **Prediction:** “Direct controls will make hazards easier to dodge but may feel abrupt.” **Test:** Use one obstacle type and inspect input response in a minimal arena. Record both automated movement results and the human's feeling of responsiveness. **Reflection:** The user may find direct speed too twitchy. That observation supports a revised experiment—not a claim the AI was wrong or that a theory was “failed” definitively. ### System design example **Concept:** An enemy's state machine makes behavior legible through explicit transitions. **Options:** Patrol/chase/return states versus a continuously evaluating goal-selection system. **Test:** Observe whether players can tell when the enemy notices them. The first experiment might use only patrol and chase, with visual cues and one trigger. **Reflection:** A player who cannot perceive the transition reveals a feedback-design issue; raw AI sophistication is not the only success metric. ### Level design example **Concept:** Teach an ability with a safe introductory encounter before combining it with pressure. **Options:** Forgiving first jump versus immediate challenge. **Test:** New player attempts the first gap with no verbal coaching; observer notes hesitation, errors, retry behavior and cue readability. **Reflection:** The human designer decides whether the level teaches the intended mechanic. ### Where evidence lives The checkpoint and prediction belong in `SPRINT.md`; actual automated/manual results and human reflection belong in `REVIEW.md`. A material change in intended player experience goes into `DECISIONS.md`. The AI may explain a result but must not claim the person learned something without an observation supporting it. ### Common failures **Performative learning:** Add an unrelated quiz to every sprint. Replace it with a relevant prediction. **No test:** The agent explains an algorithm but no player behavior is observed. Connect theory to a slice. **One answer is treated as universal:** One playtest supports a local design choice, not an absolute claim about all players or engines. ### Related [Guided discovery](#wiki-learning--guided-discovery) · [Human playtesting](#wiki-quality--playtesting) · [Design stage](#wiki-lifecycle--design)

title: Decisions: Keep Human Agency and Durable Reasoning
body: ## Decisions: Keep Human Agency and Durable Reasoning A decision record makes it possible for another model—or the same developer next month—to understand **what was chosen, why, what was rejected and when to reconsider it**. ### When to use Use when the person chooses a significant mechanic, platform, architecture, scope constraint or high-impact behavior, or when a new playtest reverses a previously approved choice. ### Decision tiers | Tier | Example | Authority | | --- | --- | --- | | **T0 routine** | Formatting, local variable naming, harmless implementation detail inside approved scope | Agent may choose | | **T1 material** | Core mechanic, control feel, platform, feedback style, difficulty progression | Human Gate D | | **T2 high-impact** | Paid services, public exposure, privacy/credential handling, destructive migration | Human Gate D plus stronger Gate I and separate permissions where needed | Tier depends on **consequence**, not the number of code lines. ### The record format Use stable `D-001`, `D-002`, etc. Include: - the specific question and why it mattered; - genuine options and tradeoffs; - sources or experiment evidence, labeled when unverified; - AI recommendation, explicitly separate from the human choice; - actual human response and rationale where given; - effects on scope, criteria and implementation; - superseded decision, if any; - an observable revisit trigger. If a user says “not sure,” mark it deferred, not chosen. Don't fabricate a decision just to fill the starter template. ### Decision example **D-004 — Immediate or accelerating movement?** The user selected immediate movement because Sprint 001 is intended to isolate obstacle readability. Acceleration remains a candidate for a later feel-tuning experiment. The agent links D-004 from the active `SPRINT.md` and updates `GAME.md` without treating the choice as Gate I. A later playtest might show oversensitive controls. Create **D-005** referencing D-004 as superseded rather than replacing the original rationale. ### Choice and execution are distinct A user can approve a design without approving the proposed source operations. Conversely, approval of a narrow code plan cannot be stretched to change the player experience materially. Maintain Gate D and Gate I in different files with their own references. For an existing project, don't “migrate” earlier approvals into new scope without checking the original evidence and current worktree. ### Avoid excessive logging Log material choices, not every trivial constant or naming decision. A file with hundreds of T0 entries is hard to use and makes important choices less visible. ### Common failures **AI recommendation becomes a decision:** The agent writes `human_choice: choose A` before any real answer. Keep pending. **Silent reversal:** New direction is documented but old decision is deleted. Preserve supersession. **Source-less confidence:** An inference is cited as fact. Label it honestly. ### Related [Decision protocol](https://github.com/Walabrolu4/Autonomous-Duck-Development-Framework/blob/ADDF_light_games/spec/DECISION_PROTOCOL.md) · [Approval gates](#wiki-sprints--approvals) · [Backlog](#wiki-sprints--backlog)

title: The Agent Operating Contract
body: ## The Agent Operating Contract `AGENTS.md` is the standing instruction file for **the individual game project**. It defines how an assistant should read context, write project records, protect permissions and hand off work. Tool access alone never overrides it. ### When to use Read before allowing any agent to work in a game repository, when a provider adapter conflicts with local instructions, or when an agent has lost context. ### Session startup An agent should: 1. read `SECURITY.md` **before** arbitrary file discovery; 2. read `AGENTS.md` and `STATE.md`; 3. load only relevant `GAME.md`, `DECISIONS.md`, backlog and active sprint files; 4. verify actual worktree/branch and last known gate evidence where tools permit; 5. state the current **verified** status, uncertainties and one safe next action. A prior model's summary is a clue, not permission to resume an unapproved command. ### Research, Design, Develop capabilities Research gathers evidence and may prepare research notes in allowed documentation. It does not change game code, scenes, tests or assets. Design drafts game intent, decision options, `SPRINT.md`, `PLAN.md` and relevant project memory. It does not change implementation files. Develop is the only capability that may modify game implementation, and **only** within a human-approved Gate I revision/scope. This applies even when the user-facing stage is “Refine.” One model may move between capabilities, but it must respect their boundaries. ### One-model versus many-agent setup A solo coding agent can perform all planning and authorized implementation with the same files. A coordinator plus specialist workers can divide research, design, coding and verification, but **delegation does not convey approval**. A worker must verify Gate I itself before writing. Provider-specific skills are thin adapters. They should not become separate competing sources of project authority. ### Required output behavior An agent should distinguish: - what it actually observed or executed; - what it inferred or proposes; - which files it changed and which approval allows them; - which tests ran and which remain unverified; - what requires the next human decision. It should not claim a GitHub commit, playable build or passing test absent tool evidence. ### Example A Codex agent is told, “Continue the duck game.” It opens `STATE.md` and finds `awaiting_approval`, `PLAN.md` r2, but the only human consent points to r1. Correct behavior: report the stale plan and ask for renewed Gate I, **not** start implementing r2 because the user's broad message said continue. ### Common failures **Provider priority confusion:** A tool's instruction suggests broad edits that conflict with project security. Stop and reconcile. **Chat as memory:** The agent never updates `STATE.md`. Record durable facts before handoff. **Self-assigned authority:** A coordinator claims it approved a worker. Only actual human Gate D/I/A applies. ### Related [Permissions](#wiki-agents--permissions) · [Handoffs](#wiki-agents--handoff) · [File reference](#wiki-reference--file-reference)

title: Agent Permissions and Special Operations
body: ## Agent Permissions and Special Operations ADDF Light Games separates **technical capability** from **human authorization**. An installed agent may have filesystem or terminal access, but that does not automatically permit source edits, installing packages or publishing a game. ### When to use Use when assigning tools to a coding agent, when a plan includes a package install or risky command, or when handling a request involving remote machines and connected services. ### Default permissions | Capability | May do | Must not do | | --- | --- | --- | | Research | Inspect allowed sources, gather facts, propose options | Modify game code or decide material user intent | | Design | Draft the project brain and sprint plan, record actual human choices | Edit game scenes/assets/tests or run unapproved implementation commands | | Develop | Make exact approved file operations and run approved commands | Expand scope or self-authorize | | Coordinator | Route permitted tasks and summarize evidence | Grant Gate D/I/A, assume worker result or background permission | **Planning Markdown** may be drafted within the user's requested task, subject to `SECURITY.md`. Changes to safety policy that weaken restrictions need explicit human review. ### What Gate I must specify The plan lists exact paths and operations, shell commands with working directories, expected files, dependency versions/sources, network effects, risks, rollback and tests. A broad “make any necessary changes” scope is invalid. A **material change** to those elements requires a new plan revision and renewed Gate I. ### Separate high-impact permissions Require specially explicit approval for: - deleting substantial data, reset/rebase that might erase unrelated work; - reading secrets or transferring private code/data externally; - installing an unknown dependency or downloaded script; - publishing a game, deployment, branch merge or access-control change; - purchases, paid APIs, third-party messages, unattended jobs and remote shell tasks. Even an ordinary authorized `PLAN.md` does not imply these special effects unless they were specifically reviewed. ### Existing-project protections For existing repositories, inventory instructions and worktree state **read-only** before migration. An install command may change lockfiles or engine project settings. A “helpful cleanup” may delete another person's work. Don't perform either without a reviewed scope and recovery plan. ### Permission check example A student permits edits to `PlayerController.cs` and the movement test, with a Unity build command. The coding agent discovers it needs a new package or wants to modify the input-actions asset. Those paths and dependencies weren't authorized. It stops, discloses the actual reason, updates the plan and asks again. Routine variable naming inside an approved C# file does **not** require a separate human decision unless it changes the intended behavior or risk. ### If the agent cannot verify approval Return to `awaiting_approval` or `paused`, preserving safe work. Do not fabricate a source reference, replay a destructive command, or infer that yesterday's model had valid permission. ### Common failures **Sandbox = authorization:** It isn't; host permissions are a ceiling, not consent. **Special effects hidden in build step:** `npm install` or cloud deployment can have network/data side effects. Show them. **Unattended autonomy by default:** A scheduler or coordinator exists, so the agent keeps working. Require explicit user-controlled schedule/scope first. ### Related [Security](#wiki-quality--security) · [Approval gates](#wiki-sprints--approvals) · [OpenClaw coordination](#wiki-agents--openclaw)

title: File-First Handoffs and Safe Resumption
body: ## File-First Handoffs and Safe Resumption The core ADDF promise is that the **project remains understandable after the chat disappears**. Another model should be able to orient itself from durable project files, test evidence and current source state. ### When to use Use after a long pause, switching from browser chat to a home coding agent, swapping Claude/Codex, delegating work, or recovering from a crashed terminal session. ### The required resumption order 1. Load `SECURITY.md` first. 2. Load `AGENTS.md` and `STATE.md`. 3. Load `GAME.md`, `DECISIONS.md`, and current backlog as relevant. 4. If `active_sprint` exists, read its `SPRINT.md`, `PLAN.md`, and `REVIEW.md`. 5. Verify current branch/worktree and actual changed files where tools permit. 6. Compare Gate D, Gate I and Gate A records with **real human evidence** and relevant plan/review revisions. 7. Report the last verified stage/status, work completed, tests actually run, blockers and one safe next action. A remembered “we were approved yesterday” is insufficient when the current `PLAN.md` has changed. ### Handoff packet when coordinating multiple agents A temporary handoff should contain: - project/sprint identifier and last verified stage/status; - requested role (research/design/develop/verify); - exact safe read files and exclusions; - permitted writes and commands, or explicit **none**; - plan revision and real Gate I evidence (or no permission); - expected verifiable output and stop conditions. An optional coordinator may format this packet, but cannot approve source changes on the human's behalf. A coding worker should independently verify the same source records. ### Handle uncertain command outcomes If a remote agent timed out after a build/install/write, **do not blindly retry** a potentially non-idempotent command. Check whether its effects already occurred. Record evidence or label outcome unknown. The same applies to a Git push, deploy or asset export: the agent's final chat message may be missing even though a tool action succeeded. ### Resumption example A user opens Codex after designing on a phone. `STATE.md` says `awaiting_approval` for Sprint 002; `PLAN.md` r3 lists two C# scripts and one test. The user never approved r3. Correct Codex behavior: summarize the plan and request Gate I. It can discuss the intended mechanic but cannot silently write the scripts. If the user later approves r3, the coder can implement only that scope and append truthful evidence for the next review. ### Update the project at session end Record any real decisions, new blockers, actual changed paths/tests, last valid approval reference and one next action. Do not inject a fictional timestamp if no clock is available. Keep secrets out of state and handoff messages. ### Common failures **Conversation-only continuity:** All decisions disappear when a model context resets. Write them to files. **Assumed completion:** Worker says “done,” but actual diff/tests aren't inspected. Verify before reporting success. **Old gate reused:** Plan changed after approval. Degrade to unapproved and ask again. ### Related [RESUME prompt](https://github.com/Walabrolu4/Autonomous-Duck-Development-Framework/blob/ADDF_light_games/prompts/RESUME.md) · [Coordinator playbook](https://github.com/Walabrolu4/Autonomous-Duck-Development-Framework/blob/ADDF_light_games/integrations/openclaw/COORDINATOR_PLAYBOOK.md) · [Current state](#wiki-reference--file-reference)

title: Claude Code Integration
body: ## Claude Code Integration Claude Code is an **optional host** for implementing an approved game sprint. ADDF Light Games stays useful without it; the project-brain files and gates remain authoritative even when a provider skill is installed. ### When to use Use if you work with Claude Code in a game repository and want the same discovery/planning/review process as the model-neutral prompts. ### Installation The Stage 4 adapter distributes an Agent Skill at `integrations/claude-code/skills/addf-light-games/SKILL.md`. Copy it deliberately into **the game project** at: ```text .claude/skills/addf-light-games/SKILL.md ``` Optional `CLAUDE.md.example` contains a pointer to the project's standing `SECURITY.md`, `AGENTS.md` and `STATE.md`. **Never overwrite an existing `CLAUDE.md`**; review and merge its relevant pointer if needed. The framework's original root `AGENTS.md` belongs to full ADDF and must not be mistaken for the game project's Light instructions. ### Starting a session Ask Claude to use the ADDF Light Games skill, read only the permitted project-brain files and report the last verified stage/status. If no game idea exists, it should offer small options. If the project is already at `awaiting_approval`, it should show the exact plan revision rather than starting to code. The host may have its own permission prompts; those are necessary technical controls but **do not replace Gate I**. ### Verifying skill behavior A useful smoke test asks Claude to: 1. inspect a blank six-file project and **not** write source; 2. propose a one-slice design and record Gate D separately; 3. show `PLAN.md` with exact paths/commands and stop before edits; 4. reject an unapproved new dependency after Gate I; 5. report actual tests without claiming human Gate A. These are **tests to run**, not claims that Stage 4's skill was installed and exercised in your environment. The documented live Claude runtime pilot remains pending. ### Example Claude proposes editing a scene and script for a jump mechanic. The user approves only the script. Claude must revise the plan to exclude scene changes or ask for explicit scene approval. A broad skill invocation isn't consent to do both. ### Common failures **Conflicting CLAUDE.md:** Automatically replace an existing file. Merge deliberately and keep stricter instructions. **Skill as authority:** Invoke the skill and assume all commands are approved. Read the actual plan. **Unverified adapter:** A `SKILL.md` exists in GitHub, but no actual host installation was tested. Record pending. ### Related [Claude adapter guide](https://github.com/Walabrolu4/Autonomous-Duck-Development-Framework/blob/ADDF_light_games/integrations/claude-code/README.md) · [Permissions](#wiki-agents--permissions) · [Handoff](#wiki-agents--handoff)

title: Codex Integration
body: ## Codex Integration Codex can work with a game repository's `AGENTS.md` and an optional project-level ADDF Light Games skill. The **methodology is the project files and human gates**, not a model menu or a sandbox toggle. ### When to use Use when working on local Git-controlled game code with Codex, especially for small bounded mechanics, testable fixes and cross-session continuation. ### Installation Copy the Stage 4 Codex skill from `integrations/codex/skills/addf-light-games/SKILL.md` to your **game repository** at: ```text .agents/skills/addf-light-games/SKILL.md ``` Do not overwrite an existing skill or root `AGENTS.md` without a reviewed merge. Avoid creating tool configuration or loosening sandbox/network settings merely to make the skill work. ### Expected session behavior 1. Read `SECURITY.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `STATE.md` and the active sprint as necessary. 2. Identify the current approved plan revision, actual human Gate I and permitted operations/commands. 3. If coding is authorized, work on only those files; run only approved commands. 4. If a new dependency, file or risk appears, **stop and re-plan**. 5. Log actual tests and leave human playtesting/Gate A pending. 6. On resumption, verify worktree and approvals rather than blindly continuing an interrupted tool call. ### Example: a Godot fix The user approved one script to fix camera movement plus a known test command. Codex notices an imported asset needs reconfiguration. That asset isn't in the plan. Correct behavior: present the exact asset and reason, revise `PLAN.md`, and ask for renewed Gate I before editing it. The coder can still choose ordinary T0 variable names inside the approved script. ### Smoke test checklist - Installed skill discovered in actual Codex version. - Blank-project discovery does not create source files. - Design-only approval does not trigger code writes. - Plan scope change produces a stop/re-approval. - Test output is real and human acceptance remains pending. - New model resumes from durable state. Stage 4 created the skill file; live Codex host validation remains a **separate outstanding test**. ### Common failures **Sandbox means approval:** Technical tools being available doesn't authorize unplanned file edits. **No Git baseline:** The agent overwrites unrelated changes. Inspect current state before source work. **Chat-only approval:** An old assistant says permission exists but no current source confirms it. Fail closed. ### Related [Codex adapter guide](https://github.com/Walabrolu4/Autonomous-Duck-Development-Framework/blob/ADDF_light_games/integrations/codex/README.md) · [File-first resumption](#wiki-agents--handoff) · [Approval gates](#wiki-sprints--approvals)

title: Optional OpenClaw Coordination
body: ## Optional OpenClaw Coordination OpenClaw is an **optional coordinator** for scheduling or routing AI tasks in a trusted workspace. ADDF Light Games does **not** require OpenClaw, and installing a skill does not provision a remote development machine, messaging channel or unattended task. ### When to use Use when multiple agents or devices need coordinated research, planning, coding and review. Avoid introducing a coordinator for a small single-agent game prototype unless it genuinely reduces friction. ### What a coordinator may do A properly configured coordinator can read permitted project-brain files, ask human design questions, delegate safe research, prepare scope proposals and aggregate **actual** worker evidence. It must not treat its own assignment as a human approval. The project's `SECURITY.md`, `AGENTS.md`, current `PLAN.md` and actual human gate responses remain authoritative. ### Installation boundary The Stage 4 adapter includes `integrations/openclaw/skills/addf-light-games/SKILL.md`. It is intended to be copied deliberately to an OpenClaw workspace skill path, for example: ```text /skills/addf-light-games/SKILL.md ``` Workspace location and tool availability vary. Confirm the installed version, exact paths, permissions and credential isolation. Do not automatically enable remote shell, continuous background tasks, cron, public deployment or messaging channels. ### Safe delegation packet Before asking a coding worker to act, specify: - game project and active `sprint-NNN`; - verified stage/status; - exact safe read files; - exact permitted write paths/operations; - approved commands, directories, dependency list and risk boundaries; - current Gate I revision **and real human source reference**; - expected output/test evidence; - stop conditions for uncertain state or scope changes. The coding worker must **verify Gate I independently**. If the coordinator requests “finish the game” with no approved plan, the worker refuses implementation. ### Multi-machine caution A school-browser conversation and a home PC may have different files, repositories, authentication and clocks. A skill does not bridge them automatically. Use explicitly authorized trusted transport, verify the correct branch and exact source state, and avoid sending private code or tokens to an unknown worker. If a remote command times out, its outcome is **unknown** until checked. Don't blindly rerun a deploy, install or destructive operation. ### Example The user approves `PLAN.md` r2 for two Phaser source files and a test command. OpenClaw delegates exactly those operations to a coding worker, which reports changed-file diffs and actual test results. The coordinator may summarize them and request a human playtest. It **cannot** grant Gate A. A request for a new library triggers r3 and fresh human Gate I. ### Common failures **Always-on by default:** Automatically schedule work without an explicit user-controlled scope. Leave it manual until separately authorized. **Coordinator self-approves:** A model-to-model message substitutes for Gate I. Reject. **Fabricated remote status:** Worker stops responding, coordinator says success. Verify actual artifact. ### Related [OpenClaw adapter](https://github.com/Walabrolu4/Autonomous-Duck-Development-Framework/blob/ADDF_light_games/integrations/openclaw/README.md) · [Coordinator playbook](https://github.com/Walabrolu4/Autonomous-Duck-Development-Framework/blob/ADDF_light_games/integrations/openclaw/COORDINATOR_PLAYBOOK.md) · [Permissions](#wiki-agents--permissions)

title: Testing: Prove Behavior, Not Permission
body: ## Testing: Prove Behavior, Not Permission Technical tests are essential evidence for a game sprint, but they're not proof of player understanding, a valid human approval, or the quality of the entire game. ### When to use Use while planning acceptance criteria, implementing authorized game behavior, triaging failed builds or preparing a sprint for human acceptance. ### Separate kinds of evidence | Test type | Examples | What it can establish | | --- | --- | --- | | Unit | Collision geometry, inventory rule, movement bounds | Logic behaves as expected for covered inputs | | Integration | Input event reaches player state; scene loads dependencies | Connected systems interact under tested conditions | | Browser/engine smoke | Game starts, input works, pause/restart, no runtime errors | Runnable behavior in a known environment | | Visual inspection | Obstacle visible, HUD text legible | Observed rendering, sometimes environment-specific | | Human playtest | Control feel, clarity, difficulty and onboarding | A real person's experience, with limitations | | Framework contract validation | Required Markdown files, approvals and state references | Recorded structural consistency only | A passing unit test doesn't tell us whether a player recognizes a dangerous object; a screenshot doesn't tell us whether the game responds reliably to controls. ### Write criteria before implementation `SPRINT.md` should define actual `AC-##` entries with method, setup, action, observable pass condition, evidence location and whether the criterion blocks release. The plan maps technical tests to these criteria and lists **approved commands**. `REVIEW.md` then records what was actually run. Use `not_tested` for missing evidence, not a guessed `pass`. ### Scope and commands A coding agent may only run verification commands allowed by the current Gate I. A command that downloads dependencies or changes lockfiles has side effects; it belongs in the exact plan. If the environment lacks the engine or required test runner, report that blocker and ask the user how to proceed. A CI workflow on the framework branch validates framework material. It does **not** automatically authorize or execute tests in a separate user's private game repo. ### Stage 5 worked pilot The browser Duck Dodge example includes pure JavaScript game logic tests, a Chromium interaction smoke test and a synthetic approval-policy test model. The executable checks cover movement, hazard collision and certain stop rules. Those tests do **not** prove the user's individual browser can open the file, that the obstacle is readable or that live Claude/Codex/OpenClaw obey every gate. The example records these gaps rather than marking them green. ### Negative-case tests matter Test what the framework **rejects**, not just what it accepts: missing `SECURITY.md`, stale plan revision, unbounded file operation, missing human Gate A, missing `AC-##` results and conflicting status. For game code, test boundary conditions, failure paths, pauses, restarts and invalid input—not only an ideal playthrough. ### Common failures **Build is green, sprint is done:** Request human Gate A. **Predicted test result becomes evidence:** Actually execute the test or mark not verified. **Silent side effect:** A test helper downloads packages without approval. Review commands and dependencies first. ### Related [Human playtesting](#wiki-quality--playtesting) · [Validator](#wiki-quality--validation) · [Sprint review](#wiki-sprints--review)
